utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you use a document and ask a witness whether that document refreshes his memory, which, of course, is in relation to his previous answer, then that document should contain a basis for considering what the witness testified and what is in his statement to be different or contradicting. That is the clear suggestion underlying such a question whether it refreshes his memory. You can do that only if the document contains elements which would provide a proper basis for re-visiting his previous answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to put another question to you. Did you have an opportunity to see the location where the soldiers took the dead body of this prisoner?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: No. But I heard them say that it should be taken to Jadar and thrown away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And while you were there, was the body, indeed, taken away?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, what was the direction to which the column left when General Mladic was present?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Which column do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The column of vehicles that General Mladic arrived with, as you described it.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: It left for Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And while you were there, in the late afternoon or early evening, you did not observe this motorcade returning from Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, what would have been the time when the motorcade left with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, how many buses arrived and from which direction? And I'm referring to the buses that later took you to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't know the direction they came from, but there were between five and six buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were all the prisoners from the field in Kasaba bussed to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I'm not sure. There were still people left behind. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This question was asked. This question was already answered that some may have left behind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On your arrival in Bratunac, did you, at any point, receive information that would indicate that there were people ferried to Bratunac after you had been taken there?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, what would have been the time when you were taken on the following day from Bratunac to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you were taken by bus to the school where you were ultimately put, did you at any time cross into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if, at any point, you stopped in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber if there were any soldiers on the buses, securing the journey?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were they soldiers or policemen?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How many buses were there in that motorcade?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I think four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were all those who were in the school in Bratunac and those who were in the buses in front of the school, were they all taken along on that journey?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't understand. I'm not sure about your question. You're asking me about the school in Bratunac. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at any point in time, have an idea as to where you were within the town of Bratunac that night when you were brought over until the afternoon hours of the following day?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Well, I think it was a school. We were in the street, parked next to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That morning, did you see any people being taken out of that school and put on buses?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: No. The night that we spent in Bratunac, there were several people taken off the buses, and they never returned. I don't know how many exactly. Shots were heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is whether, on that day before your departure for Zvornik, you were able to see other buses around the school and people being boarded onto these buses.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since it was day-time, are you able to remember where the bus you were on was parked in reference to the entrance to the school?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: We were out in the street. I don't know exactly. I was able to observe that it was a school, but I had never been in Bratunac before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told the destination you were taken to -- you were being taken to?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: We were told that we were going to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if these four or five buses, on one of which you were, they were escorted by a UN vehicle at all?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other vehicles escorting the convoy, or was it just soldiers on the buses who escorted the whole column?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not received any answer at this moment. Could you -- if you answered the question, could you do it again, whether there were other vehicles escorting the convoy, or whether it was just soldiers on the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There weren't any. Or at least I didn't observe them. There were just soldiers who were on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us how many soldiers there were in each of the buses? Or, specifically, in your bus.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think there were two of them, and they were at the front. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where it was that you were brought over and where you were put up?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: It was the school at Pilica. We were placed in the school gym.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At which point did you realise that it was the school at Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: It was something that I came to learn later. I didn't know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were taken to the school gym, you were the first ones to be placed there; right?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not completely sure, but ... there were others, people standing or sitting on the steps, those who were being taken upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were led into the sports gym, however, were you the first ones to be put there?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I only know that the school gym was overcrowded and that there were people who died in there. For the lack of air, simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to understand, Witness. When you were taken to the school gym, whether you were the first ones to be placed there, that was the question, and you said you're not completely sure. But when you say that -- that you know that the school gym was overcrowded, was it already crowded - I'm not saying overcrowded - crowded when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Was it an empty school --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it an empty school when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it was entirely empty. When I arrived, I don't remember how many people there were. However, it became full very quickly and eventually became overcrowded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Mr. Stojanovic, you earlier asked about the number of soldiers - and that's during cross-examination - were on the bus from Bratunac. I really -- since it's clearly in the witness's testimony that there were two, and since you did not give it any follow-up, I do not understand why you repeat questions in cross-examination on matters which are clear from the 92 ter material already and then not challenge or -- well, do something with it. It's just a repetition. You get the same answers, which I really totally am unable to understand what purpose that serves. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we can clarify these issues and it will become more transparent. I'm asking about the number of people in the school in Pilica. And with your leave, Your Honours, I would kindly ask, in view of the answer given by the witness to you right now, we look at a document under seal, which is the witness given by -- the statement given by this witness to the Prosecution marked 1D869, dated 23rd of May, 1996. And can we please look at page 3 in the B/C/S, the last paragraph; and that would be page 3 in the English as well. And if I may ask the next page in the English because this paragraph continues there, and we need page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you say here: "There were no other people in the gym at that stage but there were others on the stairs and the rest of the buildings." Today you gave a different description of the event, and you said that there were some people when you arrived there. Now, I'm asking you the following: This part of your statement that you gave to the Prosecution a year after the event, does it refresh your memory with regard to this specific issue of whether somebody was in the gym or not?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: As I said a minute ago in answer to your question, I said that I wasn't sure that they -- there may have or may have not been people there, because I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then can I kindly ask you, if you're no longer sure about this, to take a look at your evidence in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I need 1D866. That's page 17 in e-court, which corresponds to transcript page 3031.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at lines 2 onwards, where you say that when you arrived in the gym, it was overcrowded. What would actually be a true version of this, sir?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Well, I said that I wasn't quite sure because I was fearful. And whether it was full or not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So if -- am I right if I were to say that not even today your memory about these issues is not completely reliable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that we should ask the witness whether he's reliable or not. Could we -- Witness, one point, from what we saw as statements and what we heard in your testimony today, irrespective of whether there was no one, or only a few when you arrived, or whether there were already more, that at the end of the story, the gym was overcrowded, is that something you are certain about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was not full, but later on, after my arrival, it became overcrowded and nobody can convince me differently. I know what I experienced, and I know what I saw, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able, at any point, to notice that following your arrival to the school in Pilica, there were any other transportation of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any prisoners elsewhere on the school premises?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I think so, because I saw some people in the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how many people you saw on the stairwell in the school.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you an exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how big was the gym where you were put up?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It's just an ordinary gym for physical education. I don't know its size.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that it's 18 metres by 10 metres, would that correspond to your memory, as something being similar to a basketball court?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The next thing that I would like to ask you, can you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, again, and I'm trying to keep matters as efficient as possible, is 18 by 10 metres the approximate size of an ordinary gym, in your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I know exactly the size of gyms. And I know that the gyms were built according to similar and identical standards in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the simple answer is: Yes, that's the ordinary size. Now is there anything you would like to further explore with giving the size of this specific gym to this witness, is there any problem? Because the witness says it was an ordinary gym. You give him measurements of what appears to be an ordinary gym and then you leave it as it is. Is there any relevance in knowing whether it was 17 by 11 or 19 by 9? The Chamber wonders what you want to bring to our attention in relation to those measurements, that exact size, where the size you are referring to is exactly what the witness has told us or ordinary gym. So if there's anything you want to bring to our attention, please do so. But you have not done until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. It might be significant, and it will be, in relation to the number of people who were in the school, and, with your leave, it bears reference to what I was asking the witness right now, and I would like to put this to the witness. Can we then have the witness's statement given on the 11th of March, 1996. It's 1D868, and I'd like to remind all the parties that it's under seal. As I say, it's under seal. Can we look at paragraph 2 in both versions. I think that we need to scroll down the English version or, rather, to turn the page over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the same question was put to you on the 11th of March, 1996, and you gave a more explicit answer by saying that the school was big and that the gym was about 40 metres long, and "I don't know how wide it was." Today you said that you cannot say anything about the size of that facility. Now, in view of these discrepancies, can you estimate how many people were in the gym at the time when you described it as being overcrowded?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Well, that means that people were suffocating or the room was stifled. It seems that due to that I can say that it was overcrowded. Now, as for the exact number, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All the prisoners who had arrived in those four or five buses from Bratunac, were they all put up in the gym?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know that the gym was overcrowded. I know that soldiers stood in the doorway, shooting up into the ceiling, but I'm not sure if all the people were put up in the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We can agree, then, that you cannot give us any realistic estimate about the number of people who were put up in the gym.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Well, I was imprisoned there. My role was not to count the people in the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but you said how many people were on the pitch in Kasaba and that is the reason why I'm asking you about this smaller space.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: But I don't know how many people were taken away from Kasaba, how many of them remained in Bratunac, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can you please tell the Court, to the best of your recollection, when you were taken purportedly to be exchanged but, in fact, you were taken to the Branjevo farm, what time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it was in the afternoon, but I cannot be more precise than that because I was walking through the woods for 15 days without food. I occasionally lost consciousness. Therefore, I cannot be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your evidence in the Karadzic case, your estimate was that it was possible that the time when you were taken to the Branjevo farm was about 1600 hours and that that is when the shooting started. Would you give the same answer today?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: 1600 hours? I think it was earlier than that. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could we have that on the screen to be able to compare?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. With your leave, can we please have again Defence Exhibit 1D867, page 47 in e-court, which corresponds to page 24158 in the transcript, which is the evidence of this witness given in the Karadzic case. And let us look at line 11 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In response to the questions asked at the time, you say that according to what you recall, the shooting started at around 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you still stand by that?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes. It may have been - I'm not quite sure - it may have been a bit earlier but I'm not sure. That would be roughly the time, as I said. Maybe the same time, maybe somewhat earlier, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, on the transcript of today's proceedings, at page 64, line 24, or starting at line 22, you say: "In your evidence in the Karadzic case, your estimate that it was possible that the time when you were taken to the Branjevo farm was about 1600 hours." Line 11 on the transcript that you are referring to us, on the exhibit you are referring us to, refers to the starting of something. I don't know what was starting. Not being taken to Branjevo. This seems to be two different incidents. You say -- it says: "According to you, it started at 4.00 in the afternoon, and how long did it last?" Whatever it is that started. That's not being taken to Branjevo farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I may clarify this by putting a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan is sitting down again, so I take it that you want to wait until the -- Mr. Stojanovic has clarified issues. Or do you want to make any intervention at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I was just going to point out that in fact the 4.00 time of the starting of the executions from the Karadzic transcript was suggested by Mr. Karadzic to the witness. I'm looking for the reference to where the witness himself gave that evidence. I haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Stojanovic will certainly keep this in mind when he puts the next questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will try to put a more specific question to you. To the best of your recollection, when did the execution at Branjevo start?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: On the 16th, in the morning, I don't know at what time, Serbian soldiers arrived and told us that were to be exchanged. Instead, they tied us up and put on the buses and drove us to that meadow where people were already being killed. There were countless dead bodies there. I don't know the exact number, but quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, would it be fair to say that you arrived there and that the people who were on the bus with you were being taken out of the buses at roughly 4.00 p.m., 1600 hours?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't know what the time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that in the morning or in the afternoon of that day?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I think that it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you'll agree with me that it's different from what you had to say in the Karadzic case. You can read it. You have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, exact quote of what the witness said in the Karadzic case which you would want to put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm showing him answers -- or questions and answers from lines 11 to 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 11 until 15. What the witness tell us is that it lasted until night-fall and that his hands were tied in his back. That's the only thing the witness testifies there. If you want to put to the witness that Mr. Karadzic said that, according to the witness, it started at 4.00, there's no answer to that question. And that's what happens if you put a composite question to the witness. So if you find it anywhere where Mr. Karadzic may have found it, please put that to the witness and not an unanswered suggestion by Mr. Karadzic and suggest that there is a contradiction. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll finish this issue with a question related to time. In your view, how long was it after you boarded the buses in front of the school in Pilica that you arrived at the Branjevo farm?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Five or ten minutes; not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that people were taken out in groups of ten? Approximately ten.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far away were they taken from the spot where the bus was parked?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't know how many metres, but it wasn't far.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't hear any sort of order to fire.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: No, I was only able to see people being taken out and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know who these people who were shooting were.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You saw them, that they were already there by the time you arrived on the bus.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your estimate, how long would it take for them to take out a group of about ten before they came back to fetch another group?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't know, but it didn't take much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I'm not sure at all. They would take a group to the field, kill them, and then come back to fetch another group. I don't know how long it would take them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it have taken them some ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After you fell to the ground, at some point, one of the soldiers approached you and shot you from the back; right?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes. They first fired bursts of fire. I dropped to the ground and a man landed on my back. He was dead already. I could sense his blood flowing. And then they said that they should be shooting everyone in their head to make sure that they were dead. And then I heard them say that they shouldn't be shooting at people's heads because there was brains splattering everywhere. So they shot me in the back and I felt the hit pass under my left armpit, and then there were people still shouting, some of them were wounded, asking for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that point your hands were still tied at the back?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that point, you were lying prone on your stomach, in fact; right?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The bullet went -- passed between your body and your left arm without wounding you; right?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I'd like us to look at a document in e-court. It's 1D871. It's a photograph that we made when preparing for this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, would this be the position that, as you recall, you were lying in with your arms tied at the back?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if my hands were tied in precisely this way. I can't remember. There were dead bodies all around me. Yes, I was lying face down on my stomach.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would this body position correspond to how you were lying at the time?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D873 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said that the bullet passed between your arm and your body through the jacket.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate on this photograph how this was possible at all without the bullet injuring you?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Well, that's how happened. Perhaps it was with the help of dear Lord. I don't know how it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, this is not the witness's body and this is not the position of his arms, at least that has not been established. So to ask him how this is possible, I would say take the next break, use your arms in such a way and see whether can you make a small hole between your body and the arms when you are tied on the back. I promise you that, of course, dependant on your flexibility, and we are a bit older, both of us, that you might well manage to do it in a way different from what you see in this photograph. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honours. I tried to make it as transparent as possible. That's why I decided to proceed with the help of this photograph. Thank you. We can put the photograph away now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There's one other thing I'd like to ask you, Witness. After you were captured, the soldiers who captured you brought you over to a cafe in Pilica where people gave you food, drink and cigarettes; right?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: It wasn't Pilica. It was beyond Karakaj. I'm not sure what the place was. They were not soldiers. There was a mini-bus and I think that they were military policemen. They dropped by for a drink, and the cafe owner came over to the bus. He brought over cigarettes and a drink, and he asked if we were hungry. We said that we were. He gave us food. He was a good man. I'm sorry that I don't know his name. I've forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that his name is Ljubo, would that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't think so. I'm not sure. The only thing that would jog my memory would -- me going there and finding that cafe. I only remember that the man said that he had been working in Germany for ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Upon your arrival in Batkovic, you were registered by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You applied voluntarily for work in order to get better food; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were many prisoners in Batkovic who applied for work as volunteers with locals or with somebody else, and they would do farm work.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody physically mistreated you personally in Batkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: That's right. Not me personally. Though, when we were working on the line in Brcko, there was this one man - I don't know if he was a policeman - he beat up a few people. I think his name was Mitar, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm looking at the clock. I also established that during the first session you used approximately half an hour, and we have now a second session which took approximately one hour and a half, which makes it all together two hours. That was the assessment. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A minute. Then use that minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you give any statements about these events at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone from those who were managing the collection centre at Batkovic ask you to give accurate or inaccurate information about the things that you experienced?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I don't remember. I only remember that as I arrived there, there was the Red Cross, they registered us, and they asked some -- for some information. That was all that happened at Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. Hasan, how much time would you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just a few minutes, three or four minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three or four minutes. Then I would suggest that we use -- that we will continue for those three or four minutes so that we can excuse the witness after that, unless there would be any further questions to him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have Exhibit D269 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, this is the photograph that you just marked now during the cross-examination by Defence counsel. And I just want to ask you: When the prisoner was shot -- okay. You marked here initially where Mladic was standing when he gave his speech. Could you clarify for us, when the prisoner was shot, was Mladic standing at that place as well or was he at another location?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I think that he was in that same spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: We can remove that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, the shot that you heard that killed the prisoner at the field, was that -- was that a normal gun-shot or -- or was it something else? Sorry, was it normal sounding to you?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes. A pistol fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, could you clarify for me what's the difference between a normal shot and a -- another kind of shot? That's -- are you suggesting that it might have been --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Silenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Silenced. Okay. Well, now it's clear to me. Yes. So it did not sound as if there was a silencer on it. And, Ms. Hasan, that this is, in your view, relevant for the distance between Mr. Mladic and whether he could have heard that. Yes, it's clear to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in relation to that prisoner as well, at approximately page 54 of today's transcript, you were asked -- sorry. You gave evidence that you heard that he should be taken to Jadar. Could you be a little bit more -- more precise, did you -- was that -- was it said that that was a reference to Jadar river, or Zeleni Jadar, or is all you heard was "Jadar"?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: I think that he meant the Jadar river, that the order was for the body to be taken and thrown into the river, the Jadar. I think that there is a river by that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench has no questions, Mr. Stojanovic, I do understand that you have one or perhaps more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me ask you this: At the time when you were in the field, did you hear shots from the surrounding hills?

utterances.speaker: RM346
utterances.text: Yes. Shots could be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, does this arise from cross -- from re-examination? Where only the pistol shot was referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the question was about the nature of the shot and I think that this gave me an opportunity to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is totally -- is that the only question you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Put the question to the witness and we'll hear his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I asked and got the answer. Page 75, line 2: "Yes. Shots could be heard."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, since there are no further questions, Witness, I would like to -- well, let me first say the following. The Chamber was informed that you wanted to express -- give some comment on the incident that took place in the courtroom today. I can understand that you'd like to say something about it and what you think we should consider in this context as was sent as a message by the Victims and Witness Section. At the same time, the Chamber considers it not necessary to hear what your thoughts are about what we should do with it. I hope you'll trust that the Chamber will consider the matter in the appropriate way, and -- even without your further comments on it. Then I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and to tell us about what you experienced at the time, which may not be easy for you. We'd like to thank you for coming and we wish you a safe return home again. Before you leave the courtroom, we'll have to move into closed session, so wait for a second. And, after the break, we'll return -- we will open in open session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As announced, we resume in open session. Before I invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, I would like to put the following on the record and to inform the parties about it. The Chamber has recently communicated with the parties about the proper use of the Srebrenica trial video. In particular, to confirm with the Defence whether it still intended to make submissions with regard to the accuracy of the video's B/C/S or English transcripts, or the English subtitles that appear on the video. The Chamber has not received a response from the Defence in this regard. For the purposes of using court time as efficiently as possible, the Chamber would like to propose that -- to the parties, that for the portions of the Srebrenica trial video to be played in court for which there are English subtitles, the Chamber would request that the interpreters do -- remain silent and not interpret the audio, but instead that the video would be played once with minimal interruption allowing the Chamber to consider the English subtitles. The Chamber's approach in this regard, as it is with other exhibits, is that the parties should carefully review the transcription, subtitles and translation attached to the video and inform the Chamber if it is believed that there are any discrepancies. This saves us from playing videos twice. This is the suggested approach, and the Chamber would appreciate if the parties could agree -- if there are any problems with subtitles, of course, we'd carefully look at it as we always try to do. Then, Mr. McCloskey, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And, just to be sure, viva voce, no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ruez, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Ruez. Mr. Ruez, you'll first be examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, as you may be aware of, is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: My name is Ruez, R-u-e-z.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your first name?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Jean-Rene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your current position?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Currently I am a chief superintendent in the French national police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we all note you are speaking English. Is that your choice?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, it is my choice, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I add to that, if at any moment you would feel that you are able to express yourself better in your own language, don't hesitate to use the French language at such point in time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you once work for the Office of the Prosecutor here?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes. I joined the OTP in the 7th of April, 1995, and I left the Tribunal 7th of April, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your position?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: I arrived as an investigator and became an investigation team leader in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the case you principally worked on during all your years here?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Nearly during this entire period I worked only on the Srebrenica case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you the investigative team leader in charge of the Srebrenica investigation?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get into that a bit more later. But is it true that you have testified in the trials of Krstic, Blagojevic and Jokic, Popovic, Tolimir, and Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, and Ademovic, and Rule 61 hearing, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about your education and your work experience prior to becoming the team leader here at the OTP, where you were in the French judicial police.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes. I did my military service at age 18 as an officer. Then I went to law university during four years where I got what is now named a master 1 degree. I passed the contest to enter the police at the rank of superintendent, joined the superintendent school during two years, and then started to work in the judicial police in Paris, in Marseilles, and in Nice, mainly in the field of drugs trafficking but also armed robberies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's get directly to your work as the Srebrenica team leader. You have in the past described the different -- as you viewed, the different phases or parts of the Srebrenica investigation. Can you just briefly tell us how you divide the Srebrenica investigation up, how you went about doing it in these different parts you've talked about, if you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Due mainly to human resources, we had to split the investigation in various phases which happened naturally. The first one was to collect witness statements in order to reconstruct the events according to the multiple stories of these witnesses. Then the second phase, once the territory of Republika Srpska where the events happened was accessible, we could start missions in order to find the locations the witnesses were talking about, and collect evidence in order to confirm or infirm [sic] the stories we were told. There was then a need to find also where the bodies of the executed people were. This task was then complicated and took a long time because of a disturbance of these graves. Then once the events were reconstructed and the bodies found, all this being not in several phases, these phases were mixed, then the focus was more on identifying the perpetrators, so the military units involved and those responsible for the events, including for this, the necessity to conduct searches in military facilities, mainly the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade, and also put a hand on the intercepts, what we now call the intercepts. Following this was also the final phase, if one can say so, of interviewing as many witnesses and suspects among the military and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I note that you've taken something with you in -- that you have in front of you. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: This is the -- the book of all the exhibits that we are going to go through during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And before I get to that, I think we should --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could, Mr. President, provide Mr. Ruez with a -- a list of some of the witnesses that he may refer to but we have their RM numbers, because many of them are in private session, and if he does get asked about specific witnesses, it would be helpful for him to have that. We have given that list to the -- to the Defence. It's something that we have traditionally done with Mr. Ruez to protect the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now the book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, although, of course, the Chamber would immediately switch to which witnesses who -- but it might assist us as well to have a copy of the -- not to know that we couldn't find it, but if we have it in front of us it is easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and we did make some extra copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the book, which I note is 65 ter 28756, that, Your Honours, you should have a copy of that book in front of you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Judges received a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you create this -- this book, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you create it from?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Mainly from photographs that I took and from maps that I created.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was this done for the purpose of trials?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: It was done for the purpose of trials and adapted depending on the people who were on trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have we, the Prosecution, reduced the book from the Tolimir trial about 25 photographs, to try to make this a more targeted testimony?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes. It is a short version, let's say, of the entire -- the entire book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you have in mind for this book? What -- what is it supposed to do for the -- the Judges?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, it is designed to help orientate oneself in the crime-scene area which is a very big area since it is 70 kilometres north/south and 40 kilometres east/west, dotted with concentration spots for prisoners, execution sites, primary mass graves and secondary mass graves. It gives a feeling of the locations of these -- these places and also a view of the terrain in this global environment and mainly also the distances between the various sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did any of the information that you have on these photographs and in your book, did that come from the -- some of the actual witnesses that we see on this -- on this particular list as well as the other witnesses in the -- in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We tried in these locations to find elements the witnesses were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, without further ado, let's get to the book, and as we do, go through it as efficiently as we can to help provide the Court with these -- the visualisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we first go to -- it's page 1 in the book but it's page 19 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we will, of course, Mr. Ruez, be using the electronic machine that you're very familiar with. All right. This is the first illustration in the book. Tell us briefly why you chose that, what's it there for?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: This is the map of the entire crime scene from north to south, east and west. The -- the blue square is the approximate location of so-called safe area of Srebrenica, and the rest we will go through it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And are you familiar with the direction that the VRS first attacked from in -- in coming towards the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes. The VRS entered the enclave from the south, totally at the bottom of this map, the area named Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the investigation, did you at various times do helicopter flights where you took photos and videos of these particular areas?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Mainly in order to -- to show to the Court the distances between the locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would like now to just show a -- a short video clip that it does not have sound to it. It is not part of the -- the trial video. The trial video is real time, war-time material. This is some of Mr. Ruez's investigative materials. But it -- it doesn't have dialogue and Mr. Ruez will -- will maybe speak to us about it. But it's also just for your viewing. And it is 65 ter 22313A. And Ms. Stewart will handle that through Sanction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So here the helicopter is flying from south to north following, in fact, the road that leads to Srebrenica town. These pictures give a good indication of the terrain in this area that we call the area south, so a lot of hills and valleys. This is then the type of terrain the people walked through even though it is not precisely in that location but the terrain looks similar in this area. Very hilly. Here is a view of Srebrenica town stretched in between two -- two hills. Here we reach the centre town, an area that will be a topic of testimony by Drazen Erdemovic, events in the centre town. The view is continuing towards the north, still Srebrenica town. Going to the direction of Bratunac. Here, in Srebrenica the focus is on the Company B of the UN battalion which was stationed in Srebrenica. This is the facility of this Company B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, just to interrupt. We've stopped at 00:01:2:44 as you described Company B and let's -- I think we can continue the film.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So then there is a distance of approximately 5 kilometres going to the direction of Potocari, which is halfway between Srebrenica and Bratunac town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Are you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, a second ago you told us what other witnesses would testify about. We expect such information not from a witness but, rather, from the Prosecution. Could you keep that in mind, that, if at any time during your testimony you want to refer to statements taken, et cetera, that's fine. But what other witnesses will tell us in the future of this case is, of course, something we expect from the Prosecution and not from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar, Mr. Ruez, with a section of a video that shows a similar approach but on the ground that was actually shot on the -- at the time that the VRS and General Mladic were approaching Srebrenica from the south?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to show that video segment and there will be some speaking on it, but we'll have the subtitles, as Mr. President said, for the -- for reading as well as it can be read. And that is 65 ter 28780. It's V000-9265, and we're starting at 19:25 and going through 21:45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we may still it a time or two for you to help us identify some of the individuals on the -- the video. And this should be 11 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We should have audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us -- we're now at 2:00:57. Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, this man is General Zivanovic. That day, the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we -- I think we can all agree we saw General Mladic on the clip right before this.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: And we saw the back of General Krstic also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's continue to play it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the left of General Mladic is Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, the chief of the 1st Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's at 20:24:6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for the record I think it is the right of Mr. Mladic, not to his left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Left of the picture, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you see General -- did you get a shot at General Krstic here at this -- at this 20:27:2?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, at the right of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This soldier is not UNPROFOR soldier. He is just wearing a blue helmet taken from the UN soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We end at 21:45.4. And the Defence will probably agree that Mladic was never able to get that APC unstuck from the tree. But I don't think we need to show the rest of that section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I would like to know what makes -- what's the source for Mr. Ruez to tell us that the person wearing the blue helmet is not -- is not a UN --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The source is here also from General Mladic himself who is saying to this man, Put the thing so you look like a UN soldier, UNPROFOR soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then have the -- it scrolled back to the text of the subtitle. No, it's further. And let me see ... It's not what you said, Mr. Ruez. That's not what I read here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Put that on so it can be seen that are you an UNPROFOR member." So he is asking this Bosnian Serb soldier to put the blue helmet so that he can look like an UNPROFOR soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This all suggests that is a Bosnian Serb soldier which that's exactly what I would like you -- to ask you about, how you know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We don't know of a UN soldier who was on that spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you interpret the words apparently spoken here, "Put it on so that we can see that you're an UN soldier, UNPROFOR member," that due to any absence of knowledge of the presence of an UNPROFOR soldier, that it's your conclusion that it must have been to -- to look as if -- that's your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not what Mr. Mladic says here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. Well, I say "please proceed," but not for more than two minutes, Mr. McCloskey, or stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the time where we were going to begin going through the photographs so it's a good time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think we should take a -- we should adjourn for the day. We adjourn for the day, and we'd like to see you back, Mr. Ruez, tomorrow, but I first would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any way with whomever about your testimony, whether that's testimony you -- you gave today or whether it's testimony still to be given in the days to come. But we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom because we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 11th of April, in this same courtroom, I, at 9.30 in the morning. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of April, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.15 p.m.,
